courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a Gaussian: position, covariance, opacity, SH color
md: Opacity is not the alpha used in blending. Alpha at a pixel is opacity times the Gaussian's falloff $G$ at that pixel, so the same Gaussian contributes strongly at its center and almost nothing a few standard deviations away.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: LL/SC: watching the location instead of its value
md: LL/SC detects *writes*, so it is immune to A to B to A in principle. In practice the pop needs a load between LL and SC, which hardware does not guarantee to support, and languages expose CAS anyway.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Interaction effects and Shapley values
md: If two stages interact, no single number per stage tells the whole story. Test the key combinations (a 2 x 2 grid for a suspected pair), and when you need a per-stage split of the total, use Shapley values, which sum exactly to the full-minus-baseline gain.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Client-side-only checks, tampering, and trusting what the client sends
md: Client input may say *what* is being requested. Only server-side state (the session, the database, the policy) may say *whether* it is allowed. If a value that decides access can be edited in the browser, the check is broken.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Privileged groups, and why so many paths lead to Domain Admins
md: Enterprise Admins, Domain Admins and built-in Administrators each control the domain (EA the whole forest). Nesting hides membership, and every machine an admin signs in to becomes a place to steal that admin. Keep these groups nearly empty and audit them recursively.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Forged tickets: golden and silver, and the double krbtgt reset
md: Golden tickets are forged TGTs from the krbtgt key; silver tickets are forged service tickets from one service key and never touch the KDC. Detect mismatches between tickets and the KDC's own logs, and evict with two krbtgt resets after closing the attacker's access.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Watching the domain, and recovering after it falls
md: Audit the DC events that reveal each attack and ship them off the DCs. After a domain compromise, contain first, then evict every credential (krbtgt twice), remove persistence, rebuild what you cannot trust, and keep offline AD backups.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: .NET malware: metadata, IL and decompilers
md: de4dot's README warns that the obfuscated assembly and its dependencies are sometimes loaded into memory for execution, and tells you to use a safe sandbox if you suspect malware. Any tool that calls a sample's methods is running the sample.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: The exploit lifecycle: bug, primitive, leak, control, payload
md: Misconception: "we have CFI, so memory corruption cannot hurt us." CFI guards one rung. An attacker who already has arbitrary read/write can often reach the goal by changing data instead of code pointers (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Rules of engagement for a red team
md: Never let the red team decide alone that something is safe. Offensive actions have side effects that nobody planned: an old system that falls over when scanned, a test that locks out a service account. Two-person integrity, a named control-group contact who answers at 2 a.m., and a halt that works in minutes are cheaper than any of those outcomes.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Case: cracked Cobalt Strike and the takedowns
md: Do not write rules for a framework's defaults and call C2 covered. Malleable profiles exist precisely so that traffic can be made to look like something else, and CISA's federal red team ran more than seven different implants to prove the point (lesson 6).

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: Reading a leaderboard: harness, noise, cost and contamination
md: Checklist for any agent leaderboard number: which subset and version; which harness, tools, step and cost budget; one attempt or best of many (pass@k vs pass^1 vs pass^k); how many tasks and trials, with an interval; and whether the tasks predate the model's training cutoff.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Why an agent cannot just replay its whole history
md: A memory system is defined by four decisions: what to write, how to reconcile it with what is already stored, what to retrieve for a given step, and what to forget. Retrieval alone is RAG; the write and forget decisions are what make it memory.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Best-of-N with an imperfect verifier: the accuracy ceiling
md: FPR sets the ceiling, TPR sets the speed. With enough samples, best-of-N accuracy converges to the verifier's precision $pt / (pt + (1-p)f)$. Raising TPR only means you need fewer samples to get there.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Prompt injection: when data becomes instructions
md: Treat every token the model reads as a possible instruction from whoever wrote it. You cannot reliably make the model ignore it, so limit what obeying it can achieve.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: System prompt leakage and sensitive information disclosure
md: Assume the system prompt will be read by users and attackers. Put nothing in it that would hurt if published, and enforce every rule that matters in code.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: A crystal as data: lattice, fractional coordinates, periodicity
md: A crystal is a set of atom types, fractional coordinates in [0, 1), and a 3x3 lattice. Cartesian position is $f$ times $L$, coordinates wrap mod 1, and every distance must use the minimum image.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Detection is a z-test on the green count
md: A tiny false positive rate is not zero at scale. $z > 4$ means a one-sided p of $3.2 \times 10^{-5}$: scan a million human documents and expect about 32 false flags. Hugging Face's `WatermarkDetector` defaults to $z > 3$, where the rate is $1.3 \times 10^{-3}$. Pick the threshold for the cost of a false accusation.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Provenance in practice: soft bindings, C2PA and the EU AI Act
md: Watermarks are statistical evidence woven into content; content credentials are signed claims attached to a file. Metadata is easy to strip but cryptographically strong; watermarks survive some edits but can be scrubbed, spoofed or never applied. Real deployments combine them.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Isolation Forest: anomalies split off in fewer random cuts
md: Isolation Forest scores a point by how few random axis-parallel cuts it takes to isolate it, normalized by c(n). It is fast (training is O(t psi log psi) and needs no distances), works on a small subsample, and is strongest for global anomalies far from all the data.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: APIs from zero: REST, GraphQL and what a request carries
md: An API request carries two questions: who is calling (authentication, answered by a credential in the request) and may they do this to this object (authorization, answered by the server on every request).

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Retired grants (implicit and password) and client credentials
md: Modern OAuth in one line: authorization code with PKCE for anything with a user, client credentials for machine to machine, and nothing that puts tokens in URLs or passwords in clients.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Storing tokens in browsers, short lifetimes and revocation
md: Misconception: "HttpOnly cookies make XSS harmless." They stop script from stealing the cookie, but injected script can still send requests through the user's browser while the page is open. Storage choices limit theft; only preventing XSS stops abuse.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: How static analysis finds bugs: taint from source to sink
md: "No findings" does not mean "no bugs". Semgrep's own README warns that its free Community Edition analyses taint only within a single function or file, so it misses many true positives in security work. A flow that hops across files, or a source the rules do not know about, is invisible.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Vulnerability management end to end: inventory, scans, deduplication
md: Group findings by the action that fixes them and by the owner who must act. Developers do not want 300 tickets for one library upgrade; they want one ticket listing the 300 places it fixes.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Commit, abort with CLRs, and fuzzy checkpoints
md: A checkpoint is not a point where the disk is consistent. A fuzzy checkpoint only records which transactions were active and which pages were dirty. Redo usually has to start **before** the checkpoint, at the smallest recLSN in the DPT, because a page dirtied long ago may still be unflushed.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Input-type bugs in real pipelines
md: Record the model id and the input type (or exact prefix string) alongside the index, and check them at query time. When either changes, build a new index and switch over, rather than re-embedding part of the old one in place.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Wakers: how a Pending task gets polled again
md: The future contract: **if `poll` returns `Pending`, the future must make sure the waker from that call gets woken later** when progress is possible. Forget it and the task hangs forever, with no error. The Tokio tutorial calls this a common source of bugs.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: What atomics cost: cache lines, contention and real uses
md: Use the most specific operation that does the job. If a fetch_add, fetch_or or swap expresses your update, prefer it to a hand-written CAS loop: it never fails, and on ARM the compiler turns it into a tight instruction sequence, which (as of Mara Bos's tests) it does not do for a hand-written CAS loop.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Who are you, prove it, and what may you do?
md: Everything in this course is for understanding and defending. Only test systems you own or have written permission to test; unauthorised access is a crime in most countries.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Account recovery: the side door around every lock
md: The account is only as secure as the easiest way to reset it. If a lost-password flow needs only an email or a phone number, those become the real password.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Tokens, budgets and when to stop
md: Tokens buy research quality (80% of BrowseComp variance in Anthropic's analysis), so the budget is the main dial. Enforce budgets in the harness, reserve a share for synthesis and verification, and scale effort to the question.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: Customizing models: fine-tuning, distillation, pretraining and import
md: Serving rules for custom models have changed over time. A 2023 AWS launch post said custom models needed Provisioned Throughput; current docs also offer on-demand custom model deployments, but only for listed base models and Regions. Check the current page before you promise a serving cost.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a workflow, language fingerprints and practice
md: Reverse engineering is compiler knowledge applied backwards. Each fingerprint, idiom and convention you learn from compiling your own code is one less guess when the source is gone.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Why a pipelined CPU has to guess at every branch
md: Speculation is not a correctness risk for your program: wrong-path results never reach registers or memory. It is only a time cost. (It can leak information through caches, which is the Spectre family of attacks; lesson 5 touches on that.)

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: The LSM write path: memtable, flush and immutable SSTables
md: Misconception: "a delete in an LSM-tree frees space immediately." It adds data: a tombstone. Space comes back only when compaction merges the tombstone with every older version of that key and can finally drop both.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: Sequential flooding: how one scan wipes out the hot set
md: Recency alone cannot tell a hot page from a page that was just read once. Every scan-resistant policy adds some second signal: a count, a second reference, or knowledge of which query read the page.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Availability engineering: nines, redundancy and failure domains
md: Nines from a vendor apply to the vendor's component, under its definition of "available". Your service's availability is lower: it multiplies every hard dependency, and redundancy only helps for failures that do not hit all copies at once.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Backups attackers cannot reach: immutability and isolated recovery
md: Immutable storage is not an immutable backup *system*. If the same admin can change retention for future backups, delete the encryption key, disable the backup jobs or lock everyone out of the console, the attacker wins slowly instead of quickly. Protect the policies, keys and access paths as carefully as the bytes.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Exercising the plan: tabletops, functional tests, failovers and chaos
md: Climb from training to tabletop, functional exercise, full switchover test and continuous chaos experiments. Each needs objectives, success criteria and measured results; the output is a list of gaps with owners, and the measured RTO replaces the guessed one in the plan.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Generating with patches: the BLT decoding loop and its real cost
md: The BLT paper is explicit: its FLOP matching is theoretical, and its implementation may not yet match tokenizer-based models in wall-clock time. Equal FLOPs per byte is a claim about arithmetic, not about latency at batch size 1.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Data races: pthreads in C versus Send and Sync in Rust
md: Implementing Send or Sync by hand is `unsafe impl Send for MyType {}`, one of the five powers in lesson 4. The compiler cannot check it, and the Rustonomicon warns that an incorrect implementation can cause undefined behavior: you are promising that every way to reach the type from two threads is synchronized.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Why one load can cost 3 cycles or 240
md: You never call the cache. The only levers you have are **which addresses you touch and in what order**: data layout and access pattern. That is what the rest of this course makes precise.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Why tracing circuits needs a replacement model
md: Attribution graphs trade the real model for an interpretable stand-in whose direct interactions are linear on one prompt. Every claim read off the graph is a hypothesis about the real model until an intervention confirms it.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: What attribution graphs found: arithmetic, languages, refusals, CoT
md: Every case is one or a few prompts on one model, chosen because the method worked. The paper says plainly that it makes claims about examples, not general mechanisms, and that its graphs gave satisfying insight for only about a quarter of the prompts the authors tried.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Estimating propensities: swaps, EM, harvesting, dual learning
md: EM can only separate rank from document if the same documents appear at different ranks, and those overlaps must link all ranks together. When ranker 2 was D, E, B, A, C instead, ranks {1, 4} and {2, 3, 5} never shared a document, the relative scale between the two groups was unidentifiable, and EM's answer for rank 2 depended on its starting point: 0.63 starting from 0.5, 0.53 starting from 0.3 (truth 0.5).

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Stopping CSRF: SameSite, tokens, Origin and Fetch Metadata
md: Cross-site scripting defeats every CSRF defence, as the Samy worm showed by reading MySpace's token. CSRF defences assume the attacker is outside your origin. Fix XSS first; then CSRF defences mean something.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Where the evidence lives when there is no server to seize
md: Misconception: "the provider keeps everything, so we can ask for the logs after the incident". The provider keeps only what its defaults keep: for example CloudTrail's 90-day event history of management events. Data events, flow logs and many SaaS audit logs never exist unless you enabled them, and no support ticket can bring them back.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Containers, serverless and autoscaling: evidence that deletes itself
md: Misconception: "we can investigate the pod later". Restarts, deploys, evictions and autoscaling all destroy local evidence on their own schedule. Ship container logs and audit logs off the cluster continuously, and make "relabel and cordon, then capture" the first move, not "delete and redeploy".

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Resource control policies and the data perimeter
md: RCPs can break things you did not know depended on outside access: a partner's integration, a third-party monitoring tool, an AWS feature using a service principal. AWS "strongly recommends" not attaching RCPs to the root without testing; review IAM Access Analyzer's external access findings and CloudTrail AccessDenied errors first, then roll out OU by OU.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: The cloud from a security view: computers you rent through an API
md: In the cloud every resource is managed through a public API, so whoever holds valid credentials can act from anywhere. The main walls are identities, permissions and configuration, not the office network.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Secrets and keys: KMS, envelope encryption and secret stores
md: Encryption at rest only protects you from people who cannot use the key. If the same over-broad role can both read the bucket and call Decrypt, as an application role often can, the encryption adds an audit trail but no barrier. Grant `kms:Decrypt` as narrowly as the data itself.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Gaussian mixtures and EM: soft k-means with a shape per cluster
md: BIC's promise is asymptotic: the scikit-learn guide says it recovers the true number of components "only in the asymptotic regime", with much data actually drawn from a Gaussian mixture. On small or lumpy data, single-point components can buy unlimited likelihood. Look at the fitted variances before trusting a BIC curve, and treat `reg_covar` as a statement about the smallest cluster you believe in.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Arrow in memory: buffers, validity bitmaps and offsets
md: Arrow is not a file format for long-term storage like Parquet. Arrow data is laid out for fast random access and computation and is normally uncompressed in memory (the IPC format allows only optional LZ4 or ZSTD buffer compression); Parquet is encoded and compressed for small size on disk. A typical pipeline reads Parquet and decodes it into Arrow-style (or engine-specific) column vectors.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inside the optimizer: IR, SSA and the classic scalar passes
md: Compilers optimize an IR in SSA form: one definition per value, with phi nodes where paths merge. mem2reg takes variables out of memory; constant propagation, DCE and CSE simplify straight-line code; LICM and strength reduction slim loops; the back end selects instructions, allocates registers and schedules.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
md: PGO optimizes for the inputs you profiled. The Clang manual warns that code not exercised in the profile "will be optimized as if it is unimportant". Profiling only a unit-test suite or a single toy input can make the real workload slower.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Why long tasks fail: compounding errors and verification
md: Task success is roughly a product of step successes, so long tasks need both a high per-step rate and a check after each step that actually detects failure. Check the resulting state, not just whether an action ran.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: ThreadSanitizer: catching races with vector clocks at runtime
md: TSan only sees code paths that actually run (the manual: it cannot find races in code paths that are not executed). And if, in this particular run, the two threads happened to pass through some unrelated lock in between, that lock creates a happens-before edge and hides the race. Coverage and varied workloads still matter.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Linearizability: one copy, respecting real time
md: Linearizability is not serializability. Serializability is about transactions over many objects appearing in *some* serial order, with no real-time rule. Linearizability is about single operations on one object, *with* the real-time rule. Their combination is strict serializability.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Consistent hashing with bounded loads: a hard cap per server
md: The balance factor c is a dial between two goods: low c gives tight balance but forwards more requests away from their natural owner (more misses for caches); high c keeps affinity but tolerates more imbalance.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Arc consistency: AC-3 prunes domains before guessing
md: Search guesses; propagation deduces. Every modern CP solver alternates: make one decision, propagate to a fixpoint (repeat until no rule deletes anything more), and backtrack only when some domain becomes empty.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pinning by digest, signing images and verifying at admission
md: Misconception: "a signature means the image is safe". A signature proves who produced it and that it was not changed since. A signed image can still contain vulnerable packages or a backdoor that entered upstream, as in the xz-utils case from the Linux course. Combine signing with scanning and provenance.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Service account tokens and cloud identity for pods
md: AWS states it plainly: "Containers are not a security boundary, and the use of IAM roles for service accounts does not change this." Workload identity scopes credentials per pod, but an escaped container can act as anything on the node. Also, pods with hostNetwork: true always reach IMDS.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Exposed dashboards, kubelets and Docker APIs
md: Exposed management APIs are the most common real container compromise, and the usual payoff is mining. Every API that can start or exec into containers must require authentication and sit off the internet.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Why a multi-turn search needs explicit state
md: Misconception: a good standalone rewrite makes state unnecessary. To handle *drop the salary limit*, the rewrite must restate every surviving constraint as text, and the search engine must parse those constraints back into filters. That is two lossy conversions per turn, and a deleted constraint can come back if either one slips.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: When to ask a clarifying question instead of guessing
md: Ask when the readings are close in probability and a wrong guess is costly or hard to notice. Otherwise, guess the most literal reading, act on it, and make the interpretation visible.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Unfaithful without a hint: rationalization on natural prompts
md: Misconception: "unfaithfulness needs a planted hint, so ordinary use is safe." These pairs are ordinary benchmark questions that anyone measuring capabilities would run. Rates for frontier thinking models are low, but a CoT that reads well is still not proof it shows what chose the answer.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: The naive loop: four stages, one at a time
md: The naive loop is slow for a scheduling reason, not a kernel reason. Three units that could run at once are being used one at a time. The rest of this course is the machinery for filling those holes: **pinned memory** (so copies can be asynchronous), **streams** (so work can be queued independently), **events** (so order is expressed without stalling), and **graphs** (so launching the work is cheap).

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: From [CLS] to a score: logits, sigmoid and monoT5's true token
md: Sigmoid is monotonic (a larger logit always gives a larger score), so it never changes the order of candidates. The Sentence Transformers docs say so explicitly: MS MARCO models return logits, and adding a Sigmoid activation gives 0 to 1 scores without changing the ranking. Use sigmoid when you need a threshold or a comparable confidence, not to improve ranking.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Authenticated encryption: AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and nonce reuse
md: Use an AEAD for every new design, generate a fresh nonce per message (a counter, or 12 random bytes with a usage limit), and treat a decrypt failure as an attack, never as "try again without checking".

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Unauthenticated encryption: why decryption must refuse first
md: Common misconception: "we check that the decrypted data is valid JSON, so tampering is detected". Parsing is not authentication. The parser runs on attacker-shaped plaintext, and its success or failure is one more signal the attacker can observe.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: MAC constructions: length extension, ambiguity and replay
md: Authenticate exactly the bytes you will act on, in an encoding with one meaning, including who signed it, for what purpose and when. HMAC (or keyed BLAKE2) answers "was this made with the key"; only your encoding answers "was it made for this".

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Layout algebra: composition, tiling and partitioning
md: Composition reshapes, divide tiles, slicing selects. local_tile picks a CTA's tile, local_partition or a TV layout picks a thread's share, and both are just layout algebra applied to the same tensor.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: CXL protocols, device types and the path of one load
md: Pooling and sharing are different. In **pooling** each slice of memory belongs to exactly one host at a time; it just moves between hosts. In **sharing** (CXL 3.0) several hosts map the same bytes at once and hardware keeps them coherent. Most CXL disaggregation designs, including Pond, use pooling.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The CFAA: access, authorisation, damage and loss
md: CFAA in one line each: (a)(2) access without or beyond authorisation that obtains information; (a)(5) causing damage; (a)(7) extortion; (g) civil suits, usually needing USD 5,000 of loss in a year. Damage means impaired integrity or availability; loss includes the cost of responding.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Writing and selling tools: Marcus Hutchins and dual-use code
md: A good later career does not erase earlier conduct. Hutchins' defensive work counted heavily at sentencing, but the plea still followed. Statutes of limitation are long, and chat logs last.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Evidence in court: authenticity, hearsay and chain of custody
md: Do not 'clean up' logs before handing them over, even to remove noise. Any edit you cannot explain undermines everything else. Produce the original export and do analysis on a copy.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Why the pretraining mixture is a decision you cannot skip
md: The mixture is a vector of $k$ probabilities chosen **before** training, and it silently allocates billions of tokens. DoReMi's question: can we choose it automatically, cheaply, and without looking at downstream benchmarks?

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Cleaning the crawl: heuristic rules, perplexity filters, exact dedup
md: A perplexity filter keeps text that resembles its reference corpus, not text that is good. Using Wikipedia as the reference quietly downweights dialects, jargon and informal writing. Thresholds should be checked by training models on the result, not set by eye.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Choosing a layout: hot/cold splits, ECS chunks and columnar data
md: A common misconception, called out by Fabian himself: data-oriented design is not only about cache misses or splitting hot and cold fields. It is about designing around the data and the transforms on it. Layout is the most visible tool, not the whole method.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Searching encrypted data: deterministic encryption and enclaves
md: Every query ability you add to encrypted data leaks something: deterministic encryption leaks equality and frequency, so never use it on low-cardinality columns. Enclaves add order: randomized columns that support range queries leak the order of values to anyone who can scan the index. They move trust from the administrator to the enclave and its attestation, and only SGX keeps out the host OS.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Disposal as a process: Morgan Stanley's drives and the certificate
md: Disposal is a chain of custody: inventory by serial number, sanitise to the data's classification, use vetted vendors, require a per-device certificate naming method, tool and verifier, and reconcile every serial. Read the certificates.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Decoy cloud keys: the AWS key canary and the Grafana catch
md: Decoy keys must have no permissions and must never be real keys you "retired". For high-value placements, create them in an account you control whose number is not on public lists. Do not publish decoy keys in public repositories: AWS may react to publicly exposed keys by attaching an `AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantine` managed policy (the version number changes; V4 is current) and opening a support case.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Testing equivalence: bitwise, tolerance and the cache-hit test
md: Determinism is not one property. Pin the reduction order and you get run-to-run equality. Pin it independently of batch size and position and you get the property a server actually needs. Keep RNG state per request and you get reproducible sampling. Test each one with its own experiment, compare at the logit level, and either go bitwise or attach a measurement to your tolerance.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Least-privilege pipeline credentials: tokens, environments, secrets
md: GitHub's environment docs note that workflows on self-hosted runners are not run in an isolated container, even if they use environments. An environment controls when a secret is released, not what else on that machine can read it afterwards. Pair environments with clean runners (lesson 3).

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Training: a weighted average of masked-LM losses
md: Perplexities reported for diffusion LMs are usually upper bounds (written as a less-or-equal sign in the papers), not exact values. Comparing a bound to an autoregressive model's exact perplexity slightly favours the autoregressive model.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Why prefill stalls decode on a shared GPU
md: Misconception: "interference only matters at high load." In the timeline there was just one new prompt. Any long prompt that lands in a decode iteration creates a stall for every request in the batch. Load makes it more frequent, not possible.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: What storage remembers: the BTK floppy disk (2005)
md: Deleting a file usually removes the *pointer* to the data, not the data. Recovery works until the space is reused. Everything in the first half of this course is a variation on that sentence.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Live acquisition and encryption: the Ross Ulbricht laptop (2013)
md: Encryption turns *keep it running* into the first forensic step. If you arrive at a decrypted, unlocked machine, you may never get that state back.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop
md: DPO swaps variables: instead of learning a reward and then the policy it implies, it learns the policy directly (the trainable $\pi_\theta$, with weights $\theta$) and reads the reward off it as $\hat r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$. This is the paper's subtitle: your language model is secretly a reward model.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Offline or on-policy: online DPO, and when RL still wins
md: DPO is a strong, cheap offline baseline, not a strict upgrade over RL. Its blind spot is everything the policy generates that the pairs never covered. Fresh on-policy pairs, whether per round (iterative) or per step (online), close much of the gap; tuned on-policy RL still wins in some settings.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Flipping writes, cutting over and deleting the old path
md: Common failure modes: a write path nobody knew about keeps writing only the old store (find it with loud errors and comparisons); deletes resurrected by the backfill; reads switched before the completeness job is rerun; and deleting old data before every reader of the old field is gone.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: The three budgets a model must fit on a small device
md: A model fits a device only if three numbers fit: bytes of weights versus flash, peak bytes of live activations versus RAM, and cycles per inference versus the latency target. Check all three before training anything.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Citrix Bleed, 2023: a length bug that leaked logged-in sessions
md: MFA protects the login, not the session. Anything that leaks or steals a session token after login bypasses MFA completely, which is why session lifetime, session binding and killing sessions after an incident matter.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: End of support, hardening and the replace decision
md: A device that can no longer be patched, or that you cannot trust after a compromise, is not a vulnerability to manage: it is a replacement to schedule. Track support dates like expiry dates and replace before them.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: L1: putting the token budget in the prompt
md: Length control needs an online reward that sees the generated length. The prompt carries the budget; the RL reward is what teaches the model to honor it.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: One input, many readers: where encoding bugs come from
md: Check the value you will use, in the form you will use it, after every step that can change its meaning. Anything else is checking a different string.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Lossy conversion: Windows Best-Fit and PHP CVE-2024-4577
md: Escaping does not save you here. WorstFit shows arguments that were correctly quoted and escaped in UTF-16 becoming mis-split after conversion, because a fullwidth quote or a yen sign turns into a real quote or backslash after the escaping already ran.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: From antivirus to EDR: sensor, cloud, console and response
md: EDR does not replace logs or antivirus. It adds a recorder on every endpoint, a fleet-wide brain, and a remote hand. Each of the three can fail separately: no sensor, no data; no analytics, no alert; no one watching, no response.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Attack surface reduction rules: blocking risky behaviours
md: Exclusions are the quiet failure. Microsoft warns that excluding files or folders "can severely reduce ASR rule protection" and that excluded files run with **no reports or events recorded**. An exclusion for a whole folder such as a user-writable tools directory turns a rule off for anything an attacker can drop there.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Combinatorial optimisation and factorial HMMs
md: Do not read CO's perfect toy score as "CO beats event detection". CO was given the exact appliance powers and only three appliances with no sum collisions. Add one appliance whose power equals a sum of others, or real-world power that drifts, and per-sample matching breaks while temporal models degrade more gracefully.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: From pairwise links to entities: clustering
md: Watch cluster sizes. One low-threshold edge between two big clusters creates a giant cluster that silently merges thousands of records. Alert on clusters that grow suddenly, and require stronger evidence for edges that would join two large clusters.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: App registrations vs service principals: how an app gets an identity
md: An app is defined once (application object, home tenant) and instantiated per tenant (service principal). Credentials live with the definition, permissions with the instance. Anyone who can add a credential to a powerful app becomes that app.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Device code phishing: Storm-2372 and signing in for someone else
md: In device code flow, the tokens go to whoever started the flow, not to whoever signed in. Block it with a Conditional Access authentication flows policy except where a known device needs it, and hunt for deviceCode in sign-in logs followed by device registrations.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Hybrid identity: Entra Connect, PTA, Seamless SSO and Tier 0
md: Every component that bridges AD to Entra ID (the sync server and its accounts, PTA agents, the AZUREADSSOACC key, AD FS) can create or impersonate cloud identities. Treat each as Tier 0, roll the Seamless SSO key at least every 30 days, and keep cloud admins cloud-only.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
md: Draining one busy descriptor to `EAGAIN` can starve the others, since a fast sender may never let the buffer empty. epoll(7) suggests keeping your own ready list: mark the connection ready, process a bounded chunk, and round-robin across all ready connections before waiting again.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals by bootstrapping over queries
md: A confidence interval or significance test computed on the same queries you used to pick the winner is not valid. Report CIs from a set that played no part in the choice.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: ASLR and PIE: moving the targets on every run
md: Common misconception: "ASLR makes the overflow fail." It does not stop the corruption at all; the attacker still overwrites the pointer. ASLR only makes the *value* they write likely to be wrong. Anything that tells them the right value (next lesson) cancels it.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Putting a price on the ping-pong
md: Simplified model: real chips overlap work with store buffers (queues that hold a core's writes while it keeps running) and out-of-order execution (running later independent instructions while an earlier one waits), prefetch lines before they are asked for, and have varying transfer latency by core distance. Use the model for direction and scaling, and measure the actual number on your hardware.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: What the server sees: secure aggregation, DP, and Flower
md: Secure aggregation hides *who contributed what*. It does not make the result safe to publish: the sum of 100 updates can still reveal a rare phrase typed by one user. For that you need noise, and a budget that accounts for every round you release.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Aux-loss-free balancing: steer the router with a bias
md: The bias changes **which** experts a token uses, never **how much** a chosen expert contributes, and it receives no gradient. That is how Loss-Free Balancing controls load without fighting the language-modeling objective.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: The page table is a block-sparse matrix
md: Two classic bugs. First, `kv_last_page_len` is never 0: a request with exactly 8 tokens and page size 4 has 2 pages and last length 4. Second, FlashInfer does not allocate or free pages. Its FAQ says page-table management is the serving engine's job; FlashInfer only computes attention over whatever arrays you pass (int32, per the docs).

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: TLA+ basics: a system is states plus allowed steps
md: A primed equation is not an assignment; an action is a true-or-false formula about a pair of states. If an action says nothing about a variable, the next value is unconstrained. TLC refuses such a spec: dropping `UNCHANGED tmp` from Write makes it stop with "Successor state is not completely specified by action Write".

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Verus on real data: views, quantifiers, triggers and failed proofs
md: Write quantified specs so that the terms your proof naturally mentions match the triggers. Relate arbitrary pairs (v[i] <= v[j]) rather than neighbors when the code jumps around, and keep nonlinear or bitwise facts in small by(...) queries.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Fine-grained FP8 at scale: tiles, blocks and FP32 promotion
md: Not every tensor tolerates coarse grouping. DeepSeek tried quantizing activation gradients in 128x128 blocks (so only a transpose would be needed in the backward pass). A 16B MoE model trained for about 300B tokens diverged: Dgrad feeds every earlier layer in a chain and is very precision-sensitive. Activation gradients keep fine 1x128 tiles.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Abuse economics: make every attempt cost more than it earns
md: Profit per attempt is $s\,v - c$. Every control you add should be able to say which of the three it moves, and by how much, and what it costs honest users.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: CAPTCHAs, their limits and privacy-preserving tokens
md: A CAPTCHA is a price, not a wall. Verify it on the server, bind it to the action, make it single use, show it only when risk is high, and watch its solve rate for signs it has been broken.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Card testing, 3-D Secure and strong customer authentication
md: Card testing costs you even when every attempt is declined. Protect every endpoint that can touch a card with server-verified challenges and shaped rate limits, and use 3-D Secure to move risky card-not-present payments onto the issuer's authentication.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Fake reviews and content abuse
md: Inauthentic content shows as copies and groups: near-duplicate text, bursts, and lockstep reviewer sets. Known harmful media is matched with perceptual hashes against shared lists, never by collecting it yourself.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Trading latency for throughput: commit_delay and async commit
md: `synchronous_commit = off` and `fsync = off` sound similar but are not. The first may lose the last ~600 ms (by default) of acknowledged commits and stays consistent. The second can corrupt the whole cluster (PostgreSQL's word for all the databases one server manages) and is only for data you can recreate, such as an initial bulk load.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Measuring fuzzers honestly: coverage, crashes and statistics
md: "Unique crashes" is not a bug count. When a tool, a vendor pitch or your own dashboard reports it, ask how deduplication was done and how many distinct fixes the crashes needed.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: AI-assisted vulnerability discovery: what is verified so far
md: Verified so far: AI agents can find real bugs by variant analysis (Big Sleep, SQLite), AI-written harnesses extend fuzzing coverage and find real CVEs (OSS-Fuzz, OpenSSL), and attackers use AI to find logic flaws (GTIG 2026). In every defensive case, a concrete reproducer and a sanitizer or test confirmed the bug.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Levenshtein automata, SymSpell and fuzzy queries in production
md: Lucene's javadoc documents a surprise: `FuzzyQuery` on `abcd` with `maxEdits=2` does not match the indexed term `ab`, even though the Levenshtein distance is 2. Engines add rules of their own on top of the textbook distance, so test short terms and other edge cases directly.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: From an accepted match to a WCS header, and the triangle alternative
md: A match is not the end product. The solver turns matched star pairs into CRPIX, CRVAL and a CD matrix under a TAN projection, which any FITS tool can then use to label every pixel with RA and Dec.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Resize: the half-pixel center, worked on a four-pixel row
md: A common misconception is that interpolation conventions only matter for image quality. They also move geometry. If training resized with half-pixel centers and inference resizes without them, every pixel coordinate the model predicts is offset by $(s-1)/2$ source pixels, and no amount of retraining the head (the final prediction layers) fixes a preprocessing mismatch.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Streams: when a freed block is safe to reuse
md: Forgetting record_stream (or calling s0.wait_stream(s1) before the free, which makes all later work on s0 wait for the work already queued on s1) is a silent data race, not a crash: the new tensor's kernel on s0 may overwrite memory that s1 is still reading. The PyTorch docs note the synchronization is needed even when the side stream only writes.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Misalignment, strides and effective bandwidth
md: **Misconception:** the L1 cache makes access patterns irrelevant. Caches help when nearby warps reuse what was over-fetched, as with small misalignments. A large stride over data read once gets no reuse, and every unused byte still crosses the DRAM interface.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Occupancy: what it buys and what caps it
md: Occupancy is a capability, not an achievement. 100 percent occupancy with 5 percent of peak throughput is a latency-bound kernel with plenty of warps and nothing for them to do, and the fix has nothing to do with occupancy.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Occupancy: how many warps fit on an SM at once
md: Higher occupancy is not automatically faster. Low occupancy hurts latency hiding, but past some point extra warps add nothing, and a lower-occupancy kernel can keep more data in registers and avoid spilling (storing values that do not fit in registers out in slower memory). Measure.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: What GraphRAG costs and how its gains were measured
md: Do not estimate GraphRAG cost from the number of documents alone. Cost scales with total tokens, chunk size, gleaning rounds, the number of entities and relationships that need summaries, and the number of communities. The official docs open with a warning that GraphRAG can consume a lot of LLM resources and suggest starting small.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Build it: GRPO on GSM8K with a small model
md: A reward curve can rise while accuracy does not. If the format reward is easier to earn than the accuracy reward, the summed reward climbs as the model learns the tags, and the accuracy part stays flat. Always log each reward function separately, and evaluate on held-out questions with sampling settings you also use at test time.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Polling, caching and data quality in production
md: A common bug is merging realtime messages instead of replacing state. With FULL_DATASET, a trip missing from the newest message must lose its prediction. Merging keeps stale predictions alive for trips that already finished or were dropped by the producer.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Melissa and ILOVEYOU: viruses that used your address book
md: A blocklist of bad extensions (what the 2000 patch began with) needs constant updating and misses new types. Gateways today block by default and allow a short list of needed types, open documents in protected sandboxes, and Microsoft Office now [blocks macros in files from the internet](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365-apps/security/internet-macros-blocked) by default.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Leaks: Snowden, the Shadow Brokers and keeping bugs secret
md: Leaks change risk calculations. Snowden's disclosures pushed internet standards towards encryption by default (RFC 7258). The Shadow Brokers showed that withheld vulnerabilities can escape, which is why governments now publish their rules for disclosure (the VEP charter) and why defenders treat every critical patch as if exploit code will appear soon.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Why a flame graph shows where time goes but not why
md: Time profiles answer *where*. Counters answer *why*: low IPC plus many cache misses points at memory, many branch misses points at prediction, high IPC with lots of instructions points at doing too much work.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Power, EM, sound and faults: physical side channels
md: Physical side channels need the attacker close to the device, but that is exactly the threat model of smart cards, phones, payment terminals, hardware wallets and secure enclaves. Hertzbleed shows the line between physical and remote is not fixed: when power controls frequency, power becomes timing.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: What a desync enables, and what defenders see
md: Desync detection is a comparison problem. Log a connection or request identifier at both the front end and the back end, and alert when the request counts or request lines for the same connection differ.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: Detecting, responding, and practising safely
md: Desync and cache attacks are the same lesson twice: when two components interpret one message differently, an attacker chooses the difference. Remove ambiguity (HTTP/2 upstream, strict parsing, origin-declared caching), detect disagreement by comparing tiers, and clean up stored state after every fix.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Choosing, verifying and debugging huge pages in production
md: Huge pages are a trade: TLB reach and shorter walks against contiguity, alignment and memory overhead. Use a hugetlbfs pool when you need certainty, THP in madvise mode when the hot regions are known, and check the counters, because both mechanisms fall back silently.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Local, shared and parallel attention, and converting a Transformer
md: Choosing a layout: global attention layers buy exact recall at any distance for a growing KV cache; sliding windows cap the cache and cap exact recall with it; shared attention saves parameters, not cache; parallel heads keep a little attention, and a little KV, in every layer. Across these designs the published choices cluster around a small share of global attention, about 1 layer in 4 to 1 in 8, spread evenly.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: What OT and ICS are, and why they are not just IT
md: A common mistake is to treat a plant like an office network: run an aggressive vulnerability scan, push patches overnight, reboot to clean an infection. NIST warns that indiscriminate use of IT practices in OT 'may cause availability and timing disruptions'. In OT the security team works with control engineers, not around them.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How attacks on physical processes work
md: Three layers stood between the change and an overflow: humans watching the HMI (defeated by the replay), network monitoring (raised an alert at minute 10), and an independent safety system with its own sensor (tripped at minute 26). Design so that the last layer does not share any path with the first two.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Rules and maps: NERC CIP, IEC 62443, NIST, CISA and ATT&CK for ICS
md: Frameworks tell you what good looks like (62443, NIST), what is mandatory in your sector (NERC CIP for the bulk grid), and how attackers behave (ATT&CK for ICS). Use all three, but remember the cases: most real compromises came through remote access, default passwords and flat networks.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: OIDC as the modern alternative: the same job in JSON
md: SAML and OIDC answer the same questions: who issued this, about whom, for which app, for which login, until when, signed with which key. Learn the questions, and either protocol's fields become a checklist.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: The federation defender's checklist, and where to practise
md: Federation turns identity into a few keys and a trust list. Guard those like domain controllers, verify assertions with libraries that use only what was signed, keep sessions short and revocable, and join IdP and app logs so a login that the IdP never issued stands out.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: PAM vaults: check-out, rotation, and the Uber 2022 script
md: A PAM vault turns many secrets into one, rotates them after use, and ideally never shows them to people. That makes the vault and its administrators the most valuable target you own: protect them as the top of the control plane.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
md: Otsu always returns a threshold, even when nothing changed. On a pair with pure noise it will happily split the noise into two classes and flag a large fraction of the image. Check for a clear gap (or a minimum difference between class means) before trusting the mask.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Declaring, severity, the incident commander and the first hour
md: The IC decides and coordinates; they should not also be the person typing commands. When the IC is debugging, nobody is commanding.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Eradication and recovery: rebuild, credentials, krbtgt and backups
md: Replication is not backup. Synchronised copies (domain controllers, mirrored disks, cloud sync) receive the attacker's deletions and encryption as fast as your legitimate changes. Keep at least one copy offline and immutable, and practise restoring it.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Why escaping is fragile
md: Denylist filters ("block quotes, OR, UNION and --") are escaping's weaker cousin. They reject real input such as O'Brien, and they only stop the spellings someone thought of: SQL accepts comments, different case, different whitespace and many equivalent expressions. Lesson 9 shows a real product whose cleaning function was bypassed by finding a path where it was not applied.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Links, drains, timeouts and a CQ that never overflows
md: Size the **CQ** for the maximum number of completions that can be outstanding (including several per request for multishot operations, which post many completions from one request, lesson 5), not the SQ. Use `IORING_SETUP_CQSIZE` with `cq_entries`, and reap promptly.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Hands on the chip: fault injection, and code that resists it
md: Hardening raises cost; it does not make a chip invulnerable. The RP2350 errata show two glitches defeating an OTP lock-down (E21) and a glitch that changed which data was signature-checked (E24), both on a chip designed with fault attacks in mind. That is why lesson 8 insists that no unit holds a secret whose loss affects other units.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Prototypes: where a missing property comes from
md: Reading a missing property silently falls through to the prototype chain, ending at Object.prototype, which nearly every object shares. The keys `__proto__` and `constructor` (then `prototype`) lead from an ordinary object to that shared object. `Object.create(null)` objects have no chain to follow.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Middleware and internal headers: the Next.js bypass
md: Headers that mean something internally (recursion markers, "already authenticated", forwarded client IPs) must either be stripped at the edge or carry proof that only your own infrastructure can produce. And never let one layer be the only authorisation check: Vercel's own advice is not to use middleware as "the sole method of protecting routes".

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: Cross-thread frees, idle caches and returning memory
md: Published benchmarks (including those in mimalloc's README and report) measure specific workloads. Allocator rankings change with object sizes, thread counts and cross-thread patterns. Measure throughput, p99 latency (the 99th percentile: the time that 99 percent of requests beat) and RSS (resident set size, the memory actually held in RAM) on your own service, with production-like load, before and after switching.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Why the winner changes when the shape changes
md: A common bug is a tuning cache keyed on the kernel name alone, or on batch size only. It never misses, so it never re-tunes, and it silently serves a configuration chosen for a different shape. The symptom is a kernel that is fast in the benchmark that tuned it and mediocre everywhere else.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Worked example: how SPDK reaches 10 million IOPS on one thread
md: Measure with the right tool. SPDK reports up to 2.6 times more IOPS per core using its own `perf` example tool than using fio (the Flexible I/O Tester, the standard Linux storage benchmark) with the SPDK plugin for 4 KiB random reads, because fio's flexibility costs cycles. A slow benchmark harness can hide a fast driver.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Why a teacher's soft targets beat one-hot labels
md: The teacher's knowledge is its input-to-output mapping, including how much probability it gives to each wrong answer. Distillation transfers that mapping by using the teacher's full output distribution as the training target.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Distilling language models: word-level and sequence-level
md: Word-level KD matches the teacher's full next-token distribution at every position of a fixed sequence and needs its probabilities. Seq-KD trains on the teacher's own output text with plain cross-entropy and needs only text. Both train on prefixes the student did not write.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sharing keys and values across heads: MQA and GQA
md: GQA does not reduce attention FLOPs per query head: each query head still scores every cached token. It reduces the bytes stored and read, which is what decode is bound by.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Compressing long prompts (SnapKV, PyramidKV) and choosing a recipe
md: Smaller caches only become speed if the attention kernel reads the compressed form directly. Dequantizing to BF16 in a separate pass gives back most of the memory traffic saved.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Eviction and placement: what stays, what sinks, what is dropped
md: Choose eviction by reuse pattern, not habit. LRU is a fine default; workloads with known future reuse (queued multi-turn sessions, scheduled agent steps) do much better with placement driven by the scheduler.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Why one vector per document leaves accuracy behind
md: Late interaction = independent encoding (so documents are precomputed) + token-level matching at query time (so fine-grained evidence is not averaged away into one vector).

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: The continuous thought: hidden state in, hidden state out
md: Misconception: a continuous thought is not the embedding of the most likely next word. It is never rounded to any vocabulary entry. Decoding it with the LM head is a diagnostic only.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Pause tokens, filler dots, recurrent depth and Coconut's costs
md: Loss of auditability is a design cost, not a detail. Latent thoughts can be probed with the LM head, but there is no readable trace to check. Pfau et al. raise the same concern: hidden computation can drift away from anything a human, or a behavior-based safety check, can read.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Error windows, exponential search and monotonic models
md: Bounded search costs the leaf's worst-case error on every lookup. Exponential search costs the error of this lookup. Tight models favour bounded search; loose models with mostly good predictions favour exponential search.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: Pointwise, pairwise and listwise approaches
md: A common mix-up: these families describe the **training loss**, not the model. A listwise-trained model still scores each document independently at serving time, so serving cost is the same for all three.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The state is a key-value memory, and it fills up
md: Bigger is not a free fix. Raising $d_k$ raises capacity, but state size and per-token compute grow as $d_k d_v$. The research direction instead is a smarter write rule, which is the next lesson.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Users, groups and root: /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
md: Setting a user's shell to `/usr/sbin/nologin` or putting `*` in their password field does not fully disable them. The passwd manual notes such users may still run jobs through cron or log in by other means, and an SSH key in their home directory still works if the shell allows it. To retire an account, lock it, expire it and remove its keys.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: SSH: keys versus passwords, authorized_keys and hardening
md: Keys beat passwords because nothing guessable or reusable travels to the server. That moves the risk to the key files themselves: `authorized_keys` decides who gets in, so audit it like you audit sudoers.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: CIS Benchmarks: what one recommendation contains
md: CIS Benchmarks are consensus-written, product-specific configuration baselines with Level 1, Level 2 and STIG profiles. Each recommendation has a rationale, an audit check and a remediation, and maps to other frameworks, so one automated check can serve several auditors.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Writing audit rules that answer real questions
md: Write rules for questions, give every rule a key, use auid>=1000 together with auid!=unset, write b32 and b64 rules on x86-64, put never rules first, keep syscall rules few, and end production rule sets with -e 2.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Linux EDR and fleet telemetry: what sensors see and miss
md: Every sensor has a layer it watches and layers it cannot. Syscall hooks miss io_uring; host tools miss userland rootkits; nothing on the host reliably reports its own removal. Combine kernel-side sensors at LSM or kprobe level with off-host silence alerts.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a fleet plan, and where to practise
md: Inventory, patch, baseline, sandbox, watch, rebuild. Each is ordinary engineering on its own; run together as a loop on every host, they turn a fleet from 2,000 separate risks into one system you can measure.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: LLM judges for generation: modes, biases and fixes
md: A safe default for generation judging: pairwise or rubric grading with the explanation before the verdict; both orders, with disagreement treated as a tie; report and control length; a judge outside the model families being compared; and a human-labelled subset to measure agreement before every major change.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Continuous batching: scheduling every iteration
md: Continuous batching does **not** mean padding requests to a common length. The tokens are packed with no padding, and only attention looks at per-request boundaries. TensorRT-LLM's in-flight batching explicitly requires packed (unpadded) inputs for this reason.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: How vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM put it together
md: Strip away names and every engine is the same loop: a scheduler spending a per-step token budget, a block allocator answering whether it fits, and a policy for when it does not. The engines differ mainly in that last policy and in how they reuse cached blocks.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Designing the filter schema: enums, ranges and nulls
md: A required, non-nullable field such as `salary_max: integer` forces the model to produce a number even when the user said nothing about salary. Constrained decoding guarantees *some* integer, so you get an invented bound (for example 0, or a number copied from a few-shot example) and a filter that silently removes good results.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Latency: the dependency chain decides, not the call count
md: Parallelism is a latency lever, not a cost lever. Running 100 pointwise calls at once reads the same 22,000 tokens as running them one by one, and on a hosted API it uses up rate limits faster.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pairwise ranking prompting: allpairs, sorting and sliding
md: Pairwise preferences are not guaranteed to be transitive: the model can prefer A over B, B over C and C over A. Allpair just counts wins and copes; sorting algorithms assume a consistent comparator, so their output can depend on which pairs they happened to ask. The PRP paper reports robust results anyway but flags this as an open issue.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: ORB: binary descriptors compared with XOR and popcount
md: Float descriptors (SIFT) are compared with L2 distance; binary descriptors (ORB) with Hamming distance. Binary descriptors trade some distinctiveness for much cheaper extraction, storage and comparison.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The ABA problem: when a matching CAS is still wrong
md: Garbage collection does not make ABA go away in general. Michael points out that if a program moves the same node back and forth between two lock-free stacks, a stale CAS can still succeed even with perfect GC. What GC (and the schemes in lesson 6) do prevent is the special case where ABA comes from *freeing and reusing* a node someone still references.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: How accurate is this really, and by which metric
md: Vocabulary trap. "Parsing accuracy" in the 2019 benchmark means grouping, not token-level correctness. Modern papers reserve **PA**, short for parsing accuracy, for the stricter message-level metric where every static token *and* every parameter must be identified correctly, and use **GA** for grouping. A number quoted without its metric is worthless, so always ask: grouping or tokens, per message or per template?

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: The pipeline: collect, ship, parse, enrich, store
md: Monitor the pipeline like a production service: events per source per hour, parse-failure rate, queue depth, and the age of the newest event. A sensor that stops sending looks exactly like a quiet, safe network. Also alert on deliberate blinding: Windows event 1102 (Security log cleared) and CloudTrail StopLogging or DeleteTrail calls are ATT&CK Defense Impairment techniques (T1685.005, T1685.002).

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Threat hunting and the Pyramid of Pain: the FireEye alert
md: Use indicators (hashes, IPs, domains) for fast, cheap blocking and for searching history after a report is published. Invest your engineering time in behaviour detections, because they are the ones that still work next month.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Attention memory and Ring Attention
md: Online softmax makes attention over KV blocks order-independent. Ring Attention exploits that: queries stay put, KV blocks travel around the ring, and each host needs memory proportional to its block, not to the full sequence.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: What a loop can compute: algorithms, latent thoughts, fixed points
md: Convergence is not automatic. The toy update halves the distance to its fixed point each step (it is **contractive**); a learned block carries no such guarantee. Some loops diverge, and Huginn's analysis (lesson 7) finds tokens whose states orbit or drift instead of settling.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Why full fine-tuning is expensive, and why it may not need to be
md: Fine-tuning a pretrained model seems to move it along very few useful directions. LoRA turns that observation into an engineering bet: the *change* to each weight matrix during adaptation has low rank (the rank of a matrix is how many independent directions its outputs can point in), so it can be trained and stored as a small factorized update.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Certified removal: what 'as if retrained' means formally
md: Weights that are close to the retrained weights are not removal. Certified removal is a statement about the *distribution* of models, and it needs randomness added at training time to hide what the leftover error reveals.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Toward robust unlearning: tamper resistance, distillation, filtering
md: Robustness numbers from different papers are not comparable. Each uses its own model, data, attack budget and step definition, and Deep Ignorance itself notes that fine-tuning attack configurations are hard to compare. Compare methods only inside one paper's evaluation, and treat any red-teaming result as a lower bound.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: TCC: consent prompts, the databases and who is asking
md: Granting Full Disk Access to Terminal, an IDE or a remote-management agent is common, and it means anything running under that app can read Mail, Messages and every TCC-protected folder. Inventory which apps hold Full Disk Access across the fleet, and treat a new grant as an event worth reviewing (Endpoint Security reports `tcc_modify`).

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Case: 3CX, a notarized app with a poisoned library
md: Signatures and notarization establish *origin*, not *innocence*. When the origin itself is compromised, detection has to come from behaviour (a phone app downloading and running a second-stage binary) and from fast, Team-ID-wide blocking.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Reading x86-64 assembly: registers and core instructions
md: You do not need to read every instruction. Analysts skim for calls (what API is used?), compares and conditional jumps (what decision is made?), and constants (what string, size or key is used?).

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Indicators of compromise and the Pyramid of Pain
md: Hashes and IPs are for fast, cheap blocking and for searching history. Artifacts, tools and TTPs are what keep working next month. Report both, but build your detections near the top of the pyramid.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Why one GPU cannot train a 175B model, and the five ways to split it
md: Every axis splits something different: TP splits matrices, PP splits layers, DP splits the batch, CP splits the sequence, EP splits experts. Choosing a configuration means choosing which communication you can afford on which link.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Mixture of experts at scale: EP, token dispatch and parallel folding
md: An MoE layer is route, permute, all-to-all dispatch, grouped GEMM, all-to-all combine, unpermute. Its cost is set by bytes per token times the slowest link in the EP group, and by the hottest expert. Folding lets MoE layers choose EP freely while attention keeps its own TP and CP.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: An image is not a photograph: smear, footprint and checks
md: Treat a memory image as many snapshots stitched together. A single odd pointer or timestamp may be smear; a finding that two independent methods agree on is evidence.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Anti-forensics against memory analysis, and the cross-view answer
md: Every hiding trick must leave the hidden thing working, and working things touch the kernel: they have threads, memory, handles and sockets. Look for the part the attacker could not change without breaking their own code.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Measuring and fixing fragmentation in production
md: Fix the layer the numbers point at. Slack inside pages (active over allocated) needs objects moved or lifetimes grouped. Unused resident pages (resident over active) need purging or decay. Missing high-order physical blocks need compaction. Reaching for the wrong tool spends CPU and changes nothing.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Why freeing a removed node is the hard part
md: Removing a node and freeing it are different events. Every scheme in this course defers the free until no thread can still hold a reference taken before the removal.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: What memory safety means and why breaking it is dangerous
